docs.title: What Is a Large Language Model?
docs.text:
At its core, a large language model (LLM) does one thing: it takes in a sequence of text — the prompt — and predicts, one token at a time, the sequence of text most likely to follow it — the response. Everything an LLM appears to "know" or "do" is a consequence of patterns learned from the enormous volume of text it was trained on, not a lookup against a live database.

This has one important practical consequence: the knowledge cutoff. An LLM's training data has a fixed end date, so it has no inherent awareness of anything that happened after that point — a new paper, an updated database record, or a newly characterized variant. For an AI agent built on top of an LLM, this is not a minor footnote; it is the reason such agents are almost always paired with retrieval tools (APIs, search, or direct database queries) rather than left to answer from memory alone.

One model, many tasks. A single LLM, without retraining, can be steered toward very different jobs simply by changing the prompt and the surrounding scaffolding:

  • Translation — converting text from one language to another
  • Summarization — compressing long text into its key points
  • Chat — sustaining multi-turn, context-aware conversation
  • Named Entity Recognition (NER) — identifying and labeling entities (people, places, organizations — or, in our domain, genes, proteins, diseases, drugs) within text
  • Image generation — producing visuals from a text description (typically via a paired diffusion model rather than the LLM itself)

Why this matters for bioinformatics. Each of these generic capabilities has a direct analog in a bioinformatics AI agent:

General capability Bioinformatics application Translation Converting between DNA/RNA and protein sequences; translating non-English literature Summarization Condensing research papers, clinical notes, or pipeline/variant-call logs into readable digests Chat Natural-language querying of resources like UniProt, PubMed, or GEO NER Extracting gene, protein, disease, and drug mentions from biomedical text at scale Image generation Producing pathway diagrams, structure previews, or annotated plots on request

The knowledge-cutoff limitation is especially relevant here: biological databases update constantly, so a bioinformatics agent cannot rely on the LLM's internal memory for current sequence records, annotations, or literature. Instead, the LLM acts as the reasoning and language layer, while live retrieval tools supply the up-to-date biological data it reasons over.

docs.title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)
docs.text: In the previous section, we saw that an LLM's knowledge is frozen at the moment training ends. RAG — Retrieval-Augmented Generation — is the most widely used technique for working around that limitation. Rather than relying solely on what the model learned during training, RAG connects the LLM to an external knowledge base, commonly a vector database, that can be searched at the moment a query is made. The model's response is then generated using both the prompt and the relevant information retrieved from that external source.

docs.title: Why RAG matters
docs.text:
Overcoming outdated knowledge. Because an LLM's knowledge cutoff means it has no awareness of anything after its training period, RAG lets the model draw on current, continuously updated information — without the cost and delay of retraining the model itself.

Accessing private data. Most proprietary or domain-specific material — internal research papers, lab notebooks, unpublished datasets — was never part of a base model's training data. RAG allows the model to reason over exactly this kind of private or specialized content, retrieving it on demand rather than requiring it to have been "known" in advance.

Reducing hallucinations. When an LLM is asked something it doesn't actually know, it can generate a plausible-sounding but incorrect answer — a hallucination. By grounding the model's response in retrieved passages from verified sources, RAG substantially lowers the likelihood of this kind of fabrication, since the model is working from real supporting text rather than relying purely on internal pattern completion.

docs.title: Why this matters for bioinformatics
docs.text: RAG is especially well suited to bioinformatics applications, where the underlying data changes constantly and much of the most relevant material is domain-specific or private. An agent built with RAG can, for example, retrieve the latest entries from UniProt or PubMed before answering a question about a protein, pull facts from a lab's internal sequencing reports, or ground its answer in a specific paper a researcher has uploaded — rather than relying on what the base model happened to have seen during training, which may be outdated, incomplete, or entirely absent for a niche organism or pathway.

docs.title: What Is Agentic AI?
docs.text:
The previous sections introduced the LLM as a reasoning engine and RAG as a way to ground that engine in current, verified information. Agentic AI takes the next step: instead of simply answering a prompt, the system is given a goal, and it works toward completing that goal autonomously, with minimal human guidance at each step.

This is the key distinction between a chatbot and an agent. A chatbot generates text in response to a prompt and stops. An agent can plan a sequence of steps toward a goal, take actions in the world (not just produce text), adapt when circumstances change mid-task, and ask for help only when it genuinely needs to — rather than at every turn.

docs.title: Why do we need Agentic AI?
docs.text:
• Autonomous workflow execution. Traditional generative AI requires a human to supply instructions step by step. Agentic AI instead takes a single high-level goal, builds its own plan, and executes that plan independently — turning a multi-step workflow into a single request.

  • Tool integration and reasoning. An agent can reason about when it needs help beyond its own internal knowledge, and intelligently invoke external tools — search engines, calculators, databases, APIs — to gather information or perform actions a language model cannot do on its own.

  • Process automation. By automating complex, multi-step sequences — research, coding, data processing, and similar workflows — agentic AI scales efficiency and reduces the need for manual intervention at each stage.

docs.title: The five components of an agent
docs.text:
An agentic AI system is generally built from five core components:

  1. The Brain (LLM). The core intelligence of the system. The LLM interprets the user's goal, plans how to approach it, reasons through intermediate steps, and selects which tools to use.

  2. The Orchestrator. The framework that connects the brain to everything else. It manages task sequencing, conditional routing, loops, and delegation — effectively acting as the agent's nervous system. Tools. External functions, APIs, or databases that let the agent act beyond text generation — querying a database, running a calculation, calling a bioinformatics pipeline, or fetching a file.

  3. Memory. Handles both short-term context (the current task's working state) and long-term persistence (chat history and state that carry over across sessions), so the agent doesn't start from zero each time.

  4. Human-in-the-Loop (HITL). A control layer that lets the agent pause and ask for human guidance, feedback, or approval — particularly important when an action is costly, irreversible, or uncertain.

A closer look at the Orchestrator Because the orchestrator is what turns a language model into a functioning agent, it's worth examining its responsibilities in more detail:

Task sequencing — determining the order in which steps must happen to reach the overall goal. Conditional routing — deciding what to do next based on logic or feedback from the environment (e.g., did a tool call succeed or fail?). Tool integration — connecting the LLM to external APIs, databases, or file systems, and deciding when each tool actually needs to be called. Flow control — managing loops, retries, and delegation to sub-tasks so the agent can keep working autonomously rather than stalling. Human-in-the-loop management — coordinating with the HITL layer to pause execution and surface a decision to a human when the task calls for it.

Why this matters for bioinformatics A bioinformatics agent built on this architecture might take a goal as simple as "characterize this novel variant and summarize its likely clinical significance." The brain plans the approach; the orchestrator sequences the steps; tools query ClinVar, run a sequence alignment, or call a variant-effect predictor; memory tracks what's been found so far across a multi-step investigation; and HITL pauses the agent before it reports a clinically significant finding, so a human expert can review and approve it before it goes any further. Where a chatbot could only answer questions about a variant you described to it, an agent can go out, gather the evidence itself, and bring back a reasoned, sourced conclusion.
